$$

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The laws of logarithms are:

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)+{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(ab)$ - the product rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡(a)-{log}_{n}⁡(b)={log}_{n}⁡(\frac{a}{b})$ - the quotient rule

- ${log}_{n}⁡({c}^{m})=m{log}_{n}⁡(c)$ - the power rule

Using the quotient rule and then the product rule for logarithms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(\frac{5x}{27}) & ={log}_{3}⁡(5x)-{log}_{3}⁡(27) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(5)+{log}_{3}⁡(x)-{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{3}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(5)+{log}_{3}⁡(x)-3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Assume $q>0$.

$\ln\left(\frac{q\cdot 2}{e}\right)=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the quotient rule for logarithms, separate the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}&\ln\left(\frac{q\cdot 2}{e}\right) \\ &=\ln\left(q\cdot 2\right)-\ln\left(e\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Now use the product rule to expand the logarithm of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}&\ln\left(q\cdot 2\right)-\ln\left(e\right) \\ &=\ln\left(q\right)+\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(e\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\ln\left(e\right)=1$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}&\ln\left(q\right)+\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(e\right) \\ &=\ln\left(q\right)+\ln\left(2\right)-1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Express $\log\left(9\right)+\log\left(z\right)-\log\left(x\right)$ as a single logarithm. Assume $z>0$ and $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the product rule for logarithms, combine the first two terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}&\log\left(9\right)+\log\left(z\right)-\log\left(x\right) \\ &=\log\left(9\cdot z\right)-\log\left(x\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Now use the quotient rule to combine the remaining difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}&\log\left(9\cdot z\right)-\log\left(x\right) \\ &=\log\left(\frac{9\cdot z}{x}\right).\end{aligned}
$$
